title: 20X Anatomic and Layer Identification for Biocytin Filled Cells
author: Allen Institute for Brain Science

steps_raw.instruction: 20X Anatomic and Layer Identification for Biocytin Filled Cells

Scope and Applicability: To characterize the orientation, laminar position, and anatomical location of in vitro single cells reconstructed in mouse and human brain slices, a 3-step process is used. Briefly, 20X brightfield and/or fluorescent images of DAPI (4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) are annotated to determine layer position and brain region, of biocytin-filled cells.
Brightfield and DAPI slice overview image
Allen Mouse Common Coordinate Framework (mouse only)
Output: Slice overview image with pia, soma, white matter and cortical layers delineated. Allen Mouse Common Coordinate Framework coordinates for cell(s) of interest (mouse only).

Draw Soma, Pia and WM borders: Circle soma (pink polygon, Figure 1) and Layer 6/white matter border (blue line, Figure1) below your cell of interest on the brightfield image. Referencing the DAPI image draw a line at the pia above the soma (orange line, Figure 1), this line should be the approximate same width of the WM line previously drawn. These annotations are used to perform an upright transformation to align all reconstructed neurons to pia for visualization.

Delineate cortical layers: Referencing the DAPI image start by drawing Layer 4 and 5. Moving to the brightfield draw remaining layers (blue polygons, Figure 2). Cortical layer polygons are drawn with the same width as Pia and White matter drawings and should be wide enough to contain the entire extent of your cell of interest. These layer drawings are used to calculate the layer distribution pattern of reconstructed cells.

Place cells in the Allen Mouse Common Coordinate Framework (mouse only): Using anatomical landmarks match the experimental slice using the 20x image to a “virtual” slice in the Common Coordinate Framework using the appropriate slice angle, pitch and yaw (Figure 3). Once the virtual slice matches the experimental slice assign the appropriate layer and region to the cell of interest (Figure 4).
